content: There is an increasing number of patients who have been on antiretroviral therapy (ART) for several years. Simultaneously, there is a pressing need to ensure timely access to ART for individuals who have not yet initiated treatment. While implementing the recommendations in these guidelines will enable earlier initiation of ART for many, healthcare programs must also maintain the capacity to address the needs of patients presenting with advanced HIV disease. These patients are at a significantly higher risk of morbidity and mortality and require specialized care. During a consultation on care packages for people living with HIV, the World Health Organization (WHO) reviewed the diverse needs of patients and evaluated how programs can provide differentiated care within a public health framework. Broadly, four distinct groups of patients with specific needs were identified: 1. Patients presenting when clinically well: These individuals, often with higher CD4 cell counts, may require additional adherence and retention support to commit to lifelong ART. 2. Patients presenting with advanced disease: These individuals require expedited clinical care and ART initiation to prevent death and reduce severe illness. This includes fast-tracked care packages tailored to their critical needs. 3. Patients already on ART but requiring close monitoring: These individuals need careful clinical oversight to ensure timely interventions, such as adherence support or switching to second-line ART regimens in cases of treatment failure. 4. Stable patients on ART: This group, likely the majority, can safely reduce the frequency of clinic visits and may receive ART in community settings. This approach alleviates the burden on healthcare facilities, allowing more attention to be directed toward patients with complex conditions. Differentiated care frameworks are essential for optimizing treatment outcomes and healthcare efficiency. These frameworks involve tailoring service delivery based on the type of care required, the location of service delivery, the provider of services, and the frequency of care. For example, stable patients may benefit from less frequent clinic visits and community-based ART distribution, while those with advanced disease require intensive follow-up and specialized interventions. For patients with advanced disease, defined as those with a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or WHO clinical stages 3 and 4, the recommended care package includes: Rapid initiation of ART (after ruling out immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, or IRIS). Systematic screening for cryptococcal antigen. Screening and treatment for tuberculosis (TB) or isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) as indicated. Screening for toxoplasmosis and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Intensive follow-up to monitor progress and address complications. For stable patients, the care package may include: Less frequent clinic visits (every 3–6 months). Less frequent medication pickups (every 3–6 months). Community-based care options. Discontinuation of CD4 count monitoring if viral load testing is available. Innovative community-based ART delivery models have been developed to accommodate the growing number of stable patients on ART. These models, pioneered by organizations such as Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in collaboration with health ministries, include: Appointment spacing and fast-track ART refill systems. Community ART distribution points. Peer-led ART refill groups. Facility-based and community-based clubs. These approaches have been shown to reduce the burden on patients (e.g., reduced travel time and costs) and healthcare systems (e.g., decreased clinic attendance), while maintaining high retention rates in care (over 90% across multiple time points). The success of these models depends on reliable drug supply chains, access to quality clinical management, effective patient monitoring systems, and support from trained lay health workers. Timely linkage to care following an HIV diagnosis is critical to reducing mortality and improving treatment outcomes. Interventions to improve linkage include: Streamlined processes to reduce the time between diagnosis and care engagement, such as enhanced case management, support for HIV disclosure, patient tracing, and staff training. Peer support and navigation approaches to assist patients in accessing care. Quality improvement initiatives that address local barriers to care linkage. Despite these advancements, challenges remain. Factors such as distance to care sites, transportation costs, stigma, and long waiting times at facilities hinder successful linkage to care. Men and young people are particularly less likely to engage in HIV care. Addressing these barriers through tailored interventions is essential for improving outcomes across the continuum of care.
